Beside the table, in the wooden chair, sat Dr. Grimesby Roylott. His long grey dressing-gown left his ankles bare above red, backless Turkish slippers. Across his lap lay the short-handled whip with the long lash that we had seen earlier. His chin pointed upwards and his eyes stared horribly, rigidly, at a corner of the ceiling. A strange yellow band with brownish speckles seemed wound tightly around his forehead. He neither moved nor spoke as we came in.
“The band! The speckled band!” Holmes whispered.
I moved a step closer. Instantly the strange thing around his head began to stir. From among his hair rose a loathsome snake’s squat, diamond-shaped head and swollen neck.

“A swamp adder!” Holmes cried. “The deadliest snake in India. He died within ten seconds of its bite. Violence truly does return upon the violent, and the plotter falls into the pit he dug for someone else. Let us put this creature back in its den. Then we can take Miss Stoner somewhere safe and inform the county police.”

As he spoke, he swiftly lifted the dog whip from the dead man’s lap, slipped its loop around the snake’s neck, and drew it away from its dreadful resting-place. Holding it at arm’s length, he dropped it into the iron safe and shut the door.

Those are the true circumstances of Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s death at Stoke Moran. This account is already too long; I need not extend it by describing how we broke the sad news to the terrified girl, took her on the morning train to her kindly aunt at Harrow, or how the slow official enquiry eventually decided the Doctor had died while recklessly playing with a dangerous pet. Holmes explained the few points I still did not understand as we travelled back the following day.

“I had reached an entirely mistaken conclusion,” he told me. “That shows, my dear Watson, how dangerous it is to reason without enough information. The gipsies’ presence and the poor girl’s word ‘band’ sent me completely astray. No doubt she used it to describe the thing she briefly glimpsed by matchlight. The only credit I can claim is that I immediately reconsidered my position when it became clear that whatever threatened the person in that room could enter through neither door nor window. As I have already explained to you, my attention very soon fixed on the ventilator and the rope hanging down to the bed. Discovering that the bell-pull was false and the bed fixed to the floor immediately suggested a purpose: the rope was a bridge for something coming through the opening onto the bed. A snake occurred to me at once. Knowing that the Doctor received animals from India made me think I was probably right. An intelligent, ruthless man trained in the East might well devise a poison that no chemical examination could detect. From his point of view, the speed with which such a poison took effect would be a further advantage. A coroner would need exceptionally sharp eyes to notice the two tiny dark punctures left by the venomous fangs. Next I considered the whistle. Naturally, he had to call the snake back before daylight revealed it to his victim. He had trained it to return at his summons, probably using the milk we saw. At whatever hour he chose, he would put it through the ventilator, knowing it would descend the rope and reach the bed. It might bite the occupant, or it might not. She could escape night after night for a week. Sooner or later, though, she must become its victim.

“I had arrived at all these conclusions before I ever set foot inside his room. Examining the chair showed that he habitually stood on it, as he would have to do to reach the ventilator. The sight of the iron safe, the saucer of milk, and the loop of whipcord finally dispelled whatever doubts I still entertained. The metallic clang Miss Stoner heard plainly came from her stepfather hurriedly shutting the safe on its dreadful occupant. Once I had decided, you know how I put my theory to the test. I heard the creature hiss, as I am sure you did, and immediately struck a light and attacked it.”
“And so drove it back through the ventilator.”

“And made it attack its master on the other side. Some of my cane strokes struck home and enraged it, so it flew at the first person it saw. In that sense I am undoubtedly an indirect cause of Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s death. I cannot say I expect the responsibility to trouble my conscience very much.”
